data.content_ref: inline:The target states that the cross-city variation in the nocturnal UHI gap is modulated by sky view factor because it traps outgoing longwave radiation, with both stored heat and retention scaling with built density and street-canyon geometry. However, a mechanism based purely on longwave trapping and thermal storage fails to explain why the night-time gap is often observed to be larger in cities located in arid or dry climates, where rural vegetation is sparse and rural thermal mass is already high. In such regions, rural surfaces (e.g., bare desert soil or rock) possess high heat capacity and very low sky-view obstruction, yet the urban-rural nocturnal temperature gap is frequently more pronounced than in humid cities with similar building densities. This occurs because in humid regions, atmospheric water vapor enhances rural downwelling longwave radiation, warming the countryside and shrinking the nocturnal gap, whereas arid skies allow rapid rural radiative cooling. Consequently, a cross-city modulator focused solely on urban geometry cannot explain the frequently larger nocturnal gaps in arid cities, demonstrating a failure to identify a primary mechanism that actually explains the cross-city variation.
